title: The Gang Gets Cursed

jokes.text: Mac reveals he has been writing Bar Rescue a letter every week since the show first started, and it's been 'too long'
jokes.setup: The gang is excited about a Bar Rescue letter and wonders how it happened
jokes.punchline: 'I've been writing them a letter every week since the show first started.' / 'Well, how long's it been?' / 'Too long.'
jokes.explanation: The joke works because it's perfectly in character — Mac's obsessive, delusional persistence is a core trait. 'Too long' as the deadpan answer about an embarrassingly extended campaign is economical and lands well.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I very much do want to be famous, but I don't know if I want to be on a reality show where they try and make us look like jerks.

jokes.text: Dennis's concern about Bar Rescue is that they might edit him to 'look stupid' — not the health violations, the criminal behavior, or the bar's failures
jokes.setup: The gang debates whether to participate in Bar Rescue
jokes.punchline: Dennis's specific fear is being edited to look stupid, completely blind to all the actual damning things about him
jokes.explanation: Classic Dennis narcissism — his concern isn't that the bar is a disaster, but that editing might make HIM look bad. Good character integration but not sharply constructed enough to be exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: 'Cause, like, what if they, like, edit it to, like, make me look stupid or something?

jokes.text: Mac says he's 'a little disappointed' he wasn't told earlier because he would have been 'working out for weeks in preparation' for Bar Rescue, then worries about his shirt falling off on TV
jokes.setup: The gang discusses the Bar Rescue opportunity
jokes.punchline: Mac's entire concern is physical vanity and the possibility of his shirt falling off on camera
jokes.explanation: The 'shirt falling off' detail is specific and absurd in a way that's very Mac — his insecurity about his physique expressed as a concern that his shirt might accidentally expose his body is a great character note.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: What if, what if my shirt falls off?

jokes.text: Mac mentions he hasn't been keeping up with his workouts, and Charlie immediately cuts in: 'Ever. He never has. Yeah.'
jokes.setup: Mac says he's 'a little off his regimen' with workouts
jokes.punchline: Charlie's flat interjection — 'Ever. He never has. Yeah.' — punctures Mac's self-mythology
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — three words ('Ever. He never has.') completely deflate Mac's self-delusion. The rhythm of Charlie just flatly stating the truth while Mac continues talking is very well structured.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Dennis worrying about being edited to look stupid when he's already demonstrably stupid

jokes.text: Mac argues they should put MORE crumbs all over the bar before Bar Rescue comes
jokes.setup: Someone is cleaning up the bar before Bar Rescue arrives
jokes.punchline: Mac insists 'There should be more crumbs. We should put crumbs all over the goddamn bar.'
jokes.explanation: It's a decent absurdist inversion — cleaning up vs. adding crumbs — but the logic isn't fully developed. We don't quite get why Mac thinks this is a good idea, which undercuts the joke.

dialogue.line: Ever. He never has. Yeah.

jokes.text: Dennis can't remember the word 'homes' — describing them as 'the boxes that people live in'
jokes.setup: Dennis wants to look good for people watching at home and trails off searching for the word
jokes.punchline: 'The boxes that people live in?' / 'You talking about their homes?' / 'Yes... Jesus, I couldn't think of that word.'
jokes.explanation: This is a great setup for the Bell's palsy/mold reveal later and works as a standalone joke too. Dennis's narcissistic intelligence failing him in real time — he can't remember the word 'homes' — is both funny and ominous. 'The boxes that people live in' is an inspired paraphrase. Good economy and strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: the boxes that people live in

jokes.text: Dee enters with visible facial paralysis (Bell's palsy) and says 'whatever you do, don't laugh' — then the gang immediately laughs
jokes.setup: Dee warns the gang not to laugh at something
jokes.punchline: She has obvious facial paralysis; the gang erupts in laughter
jokes.explanation: Classic physical comedy setup that works because Dee is always the butt of the joke. The 'don't laugh' instruction guaranteeing a laugh is a simple but effective comedic structure. High impact because it's visual and the gang's immediate reaction amplifies it.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: You talking about their homes? Y... uh, yes, yeah. Their homes. Jesus. I couldn't think of that word. That's so weird.

jokes.text: Frank cracks an egg and it's bloody — 'My egg's all bloody'
jokes.setup: The gang is discussing whether they're cursed; Frank is making eggs
jokes.punchline: Frank's egg turns out to be bloody — a seagull egg, we learn later
jokes.explanation: The bloody egg works as an in-the-moment gross-out visual and gets paid off brilliantly later when we learn it was a seagull egg he mixed up with his store eggs. High rewatch bonus for the retroactive logic. 'My egg's all bloody' as a deadpan delivery is very Frank.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: How are we not supposed to laugh at that?

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I wouldn't laugh at that.

jokes.text: Charlie immediately frames the bloody egg and Bell's palsy as evidence of a supernatural curse
jokes.setup: Two bad things have happened simultaneously
jokes.punchline: Charlie leaps to 'this is the kind of stuff that starts happening when someone's put a curse on you'
jokes.explanation: Good character work for Charlie, who is the resident superstition expert of the group, but the joke is more of a plot engine than a fully fleshed-out comedic beat.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: My egg's all bloody.

jokes.text: Dee's flashback: she went to her neighbor's door at 3 AM with brownies, 'kindly' asking them to keep the noise down
jokes.setup: Dee claims she had a 'tiny little issue' with a neighbor
jokes.punchline: The flashback shows her screaming 'Spewing my hate all over your teenage asses' and banging down the door at 3 AM — then claiming she was 'kindly' asking for quiet
jokes.explanation: Classic Always Sunny unreliable narrator structure — Dee's self-perception versus reality. 'Spewing my hate all over your teenage asses' is a great specific line, and the contrast with 'I just wanted to kindly ask' is well-executed irony. Good character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: I don't know what's going on with my face, but it's broken or something.

jokes.text: The neighbor opens the door to Dee, who brought brownies at 3 AM, and the neighbor initially softens — then Dee pulls out the 'Cunt of the Year' trophy
jokes.setup: The neighbor is touched that Dee brought her something, saying 'Oh it's so nice. What is it?'
jokes.punchline: 'Well, it's a trophy. See? It says Cunt of the Year. That's you.'
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The setup beautifully misdirects — brownies at 3 AM, neighbor softening, the anticipation of a sweet moment — then Dee presents a 'Cunt of the Year' trophy. The deadpan 'That's you' delivery is pitch-perfect. The specificity of the trophy as a recurring gang artifact makes this feel earned. Highly quotable, strong structure, great character integration. Comfortably in the 8+ range.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I call old ladies cunts all the time.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: We all do.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Right.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: That's true.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: We do. We do.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I called an old lady a cunt this morning.

jokes.text: Neighbor's reaction to Dee's 3am brownie visit: sincerely touched. 'Oh. Oh, no. I'm so sorry. I didn't realize. That was really sweet of you.'
jokes.setup: We expect the neighbor to be angry or scared after Dee's unhinged 3am visit.
jokes.punchline: The neighbor is genuinely, warmly touched by the brownies — completely defusing Dee's aggression with sincerity, which makes the subsequent trophy reveal more devastating.
jokes.explanation: The misdirection is sharp — the warm neighbor reaction sets up the 'Cunt of the Year' trophy punchline beautifully. The audience is lulled into thinking Dee accidentally did something nice, making the trophy reveal land harder.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Well, it's a trophy. See? It says 'Cunt of the Year.' That's you.

jokes.text: Neighbor curses Dee: 'You are a nasty woman, and bad things are going to happen to you one day. I guarantee it. Drop dead.'
jokes.setup: The neighbor has just received a 'Cunt of the Year' trophy.
jokes.punchline: Her response is not a supernatural curse but an extremely human, almost grandmotherly 'bad things will happen to you' — which turns out to be functionally accurate anyway.
jokes.explanation: Works as setup for the episode's curse premise. Funny because it's a totally mundane non-supernatural 'curse' that the gang immediately treats as genuine magic.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Dee had no right to give that trophy away.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: We worked very, very hard on that.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Nobody wanted to do it.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Plus, she earned it, right?

jokes.text: After the 'Cunt of the Year' reveal, the gang's response is not outrage at Dee's behavior, but that 'Dee had no right to give that trophy away — we worked very, very hard on that'
jokes.setup: The gang hears the story of Dee calling her neighbor a cunt and potentially getting cursed
jokes.punchline: Their collective concern is not Dee's cruelty but that she gave away a trophy she 'earned' — with everyone agreeing 'nobody wanted to make it'
jokes.explanation: Perfectly captures the show's ethos — the gang's moral compass is so broken that gift-giving the trophy is the outrage, not the act that warranted it. 'Nobody wanted to do it' and 'you earned it' together are very funny. The escalating indignation from the group about trophy logistics while ignoring the cruelty is excellent ensemble character work.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Oh, what a sweet little birdie. You want some food? Want some?

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Whoa! Shit, Frank!

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Die! Come here, you rat, die!

jokes.text: 'I don't know if I want to be on a reality show where they try and make us look like jerks' — delivered as the gang casually admits they all call old ladies cunts
jokes.setup: Mac tries to refocus on the curse issue
jokes.punchline: The gang nonchalantly admits they all call old ladies cunts routinely: 'I called an old lady a cunt this morning.' / 'See? Did you? Yeah.' / 'I sure did.'
jokes.explanation: The casual normalization of calling old ladies cunts among the gang — as if it's a perfectly ordinary thing — is a solid dark comedy beat. 'I sure did. I sure did.' as a boast is funny. Good ensemble rhythm.

dialogue.speaker: Cricket
dialogue.line: What is your deal, man? One second you need me, the next I'm a pile of garbage?

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Cricket, beat it, man... You better beat it, or I'm gonna beat you with my shoe.

jokes.text: Frank's flashback: a seagull flies into the bar while he's making a banana daiquiri. He cheerfully says 'Cheers' — then immediately tries to murder it
jokes.setup: Charlie describes how Frank got his seagull curse — Frank is mid-daiquiri, a cute seagull arrives
jokes.punchline: Frank screams 'Die! Come here, you rat, die! And die, you fucking seagull. Bitch. Fucking cunt.' — a one-man violent escalation
jokes.explanation: The 'Cheers' to the bird before attempting to murder it is a perfect comedic beat — the micro-moment of warmth before the explosion of violence is very Frank. The escalating profanity at a seagull ('Bitch. Fucking cunt.') is unhinged and very funny. High character integration: only Frank would do this.

dialogue.speaker: Cricket
dialogue.line: Vos omnes maledicti mille annis.

jokes.text: Cricket appears in the bar in the middle of a tense negotiation with Mac, curses him in Latin: 'Vos omnes maledicti mille annis'
jokes.setup: Cricket confronts Mac about not holding up his end of a bargain, Mac dismisses him as 'street trash'
jokes.punchline: Cricket, humiliated, storms out delivering a formal Latin curse: 'Vos omnes maledicti mille annis'
jokes.explanation: Cricket deploying actual Latin to curse Mac — a street rat who somehow knows liturgical Latin — is a great absurdist character moment. The specificity of the Latin phrase elevates what could be a throwaway beat. Good escalation from the humiliation scene.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Like, if a black cat crosses your path, do you spit over your left shoulder?

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Why would I do that?

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: You guys don't do that one?

jokes.text: Mac can't remember where Charlie's curse knowledge comes from mid-sentence — 'Charlie, how do you know all this curse... stuff?'
jokes.setup: Mac is about to ask Charlie a question about curse lore
jokes.punchline: Mac trails off mid-word and can't complete the sentence — an echo of Dennis's 'boxes' brain fog, hinting at mold exposure
jokes.explanation: A quiet but effective callback to Dennis's word-finding problem — now Mac is experiencing it too. On first watch it reads as a minor stumble; on rewatch it's a clear running gag about mold-induced brain fog spreading through the gang. Rewatch value is high.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: And 'just in case' is as good a reason to believe in anything as any.

jokes.text: Charlie's superstition philosophy: 'If a black cat crosses your path, do you spit over your left shoulder?' — the gang has never heard of this one
jokes.setup: Charlie is trying to convince the gang that superstitions are worth following 'just in case'
jokes.punchline: He lists increasingly obscure superstitions, culminating in 'do you spit over your left shoulder?' which no one has heard of — implying Charlie may have made it up
jokes.explanation: Charlie as the group's resident folk-wisdom expert is good character work, but the joke is a bit flat. The setup of the escalating superstitions works, but the punchline — nobody knowing the spitting one — is mild.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I'm Dennis, the brother of this horrible woman

jokes.text: Charlie's 'just in case' superstition argument — 'just in case is as good a reason to believe in anything as any'
jokes.setup: Charlie argues that even if curses aren't real, you should follow the rules 'just in case,' using birthday candle wishes as the example
jokes.punchline: 'Just in case is as good a reason to believe in anything as any' — delivered as profound wisdom
jokes.explanation: Charlie's idiot-savant philosophical moment — his logic is actually not wrong but arrives wrapped in superstition about curses. The birthday candle pivot from curses to relatable universal behavior is a smart structural move. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: She feels... She, uh... Oh, what's the word? To make better the feelings?

dialogue.speaker: Neighbor
dialogue.line: Sorry?

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Sorry. Yes. Goddamn.

jokes.text: Frank threatens to 'paralyze the other side of Dee's face' if she doesn't get the trophy back
jokes.setup: Dee needs to apologize to her neighbor to lift the curse; Frank also wants the 'Cunt of the Year' trophy back
jokes.punchline: 'I swear to God, if she doesn't have that thing, I'm gonna paralyze the other side of your face'
jokes.explanation: A great callback joke — Frank threatening violence as a path to symmetrical facial paralysis is dark and absurd. Well-timed and uses the established Bell's palsy setup effectively. Very Frank.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I was murdered to a woman named Maureen

jokes.text: Dennis at the neighbor's door, unable to say 'sorry': 'She, uh... she feels... Oh, what's the word? To make better the feelings?' / Dee: 'Sorry?' / Dennis: 'Sorry. Yes. Goddamn.'
jokes.setup: Dennis is tasked with helping Dee apologize to the neighbor.
jokes.punchline: Dennis physically cannot produce the word 'sorry' — he has to have it fed to him, and even then says it with contempt. For a narcissist, the word is literally inaccessible.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional character integration. Dennis's narcissism is so complete that the word 'sorry' is as unavailable to him as 'homes' was earlier — the parallel with joke #6 makes this a double payoff. 'To make better the feelings' as a Dennis circumlocution for 'sorry' is both funny and psychologically precise. The 'Goddamn' after Dee prompts him is perfect — he's angry at having to say it.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I was, I was murdered to a woman named Maureen.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: No, I meant married. I'm sorry.

jokes.text: Mac and Dee panic about a black cat running out of the neighbor's apartment — but it may be the ghost of her dead cat 'Maureen'
jokes.setup: Charlie warned them about a black cat omen; Mac claims he saw a black cat run out of the neighbor's apartment
jokes.punchline: The neighbor says she had a black cat named Maureen — 'but she's been dead for years.' They both freak out.
jokes.explanation: Good escalation of the superstition plotline — a potentially supernatural encounter that deepens the curse mythology. Works primarily as plot escalation with comedic payoff from Mac and Dee's visible fear.

dialogue.speaker: Neighbor
dialogue.line: And please keep the noise down at night.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Yeah. Okay, you got it, cunt.

jokes.text: Frank says he 'was murdered to a woman named Maureen'
jokes.setup: Mac and Dee are panicking about the neighbor's dead cat named Maureen
jokes.punchline: Frank blurts out 'I was murdered to a woman named Maureen' — then corrects himself: 'I meant married'
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. 'I was murdered to a woman named Maureen' works on multiple levels: it's the mold brain fog escalating, it's a Freudian slip about Frank's feelings toward Maureen Ponderosa, and it's genuinely funny as a malapropism. The self-correction makes it land harder. Highly quotable, strong character integration — Frank's complicated relationship with Maureen makes 'murdered' feel almost intentional.

dialogue.speaker: Cricket
dialogue.line: There's only four in here.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: I drank two of 'em, of course. / If I'm being honest, I drank four. Two of those are piss.

jokes.text: Mac and Dee's attempt at an apology ends with Dee telling the neighbor 'Okay, you got it, cunt' as they leave
jokes.setup: Mac and Dee are trying to make amends with the neighbor to lift the curse; the neighbor asks them to keep the noise down
jokes.punchline: Dee exits saying 'Yeah. Okay, you got it, cunt.' — completely undermining the entire apology
jokes.explanation: Perfect structural callback — the whole mission was to apologize and undo the curse, and Dee can't even complete a successful exit without reverting to form. 'Yeah. Okay, you got it, cunt' is a masterclass in character comedy: the acknowledgment followed by the slur undoes all the work. This is the gang being unable to change, which is the entire premise of the show. Very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Something wrong with your dick?

dialogue.speaker: Cricket
dialogue.line: If it's your dick, though, I got to charge you for it.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: I'm not whipping anything out!

dialogue.speaker: Cricket
dialogue.line: There's a tiered system...

jokes.text: Cricket brings Mac a six-pack as a gift — but there are only four beers left because he drank two. When Mac calls him out: 'Oh, I'm gonna buy a six-pack and not drink two?' Then it escalates — he actually drank four, two are piss
jokes.setup: Cricket says he did something nice and got Mac a six-pack of beers
jokes.punchline: First: only four left because he drank two. Second escalation: actually he drank four, so two bottles are filled with his urine because he was stuck in the van
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. The double escalation is structurally excellent: (1) six-pack becomes four because Cricket drank two ('Oh, I'm gonna buy a six-pack and not drink two?' — perfectly delivered rationalization), then (2) the dark twist that he actually drank four and two are piss from being stuck in the van. Each escalation is worse and funnier than the last. Mac's acceptance ('I'm just glad to have a beverage') is a perfect button. High quotability, strong character integration for Cricket's degraded circumstances.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Mac's completely fabricated letter from Chase Utley that he recites from memory, including embarrassing personal details

jokes.text: Mac reveals the monkey paw — 'it's good luck, like a rabbit's foot' — and Cricket points out the theological inconsistency with Mac's God beliefs
jokes.setup: Mac shows Cricket a severed monkey paw he's been carrying for luck
jokes.punchline: Cricket: 'Sorry, I thought God was the reason anything good happens, et cetera.' Mac tries to explain the theological compatibility and Cricket: 'It makes literally no sense. You got to pick a lane.'
jokes.explanation: Cricket calling out Mac's theological inconsistency is a great reversal — the disgraced street person is the voice of logical consistency against Mac's tortured God-and-luck reconciliation. 'Pick a lane' is a good button. Good character work for both.

dialogue.speaker: Chase
dialogue.line: I thought Mac was a little kid.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: There's a child. A child born unto me. Little Mac. / He's Little Mac, I'm Big Mac, and you shall have a catch with him.

jokes.text: Mac's explanation of God's role: 'God decides who the good things happen to and then who he smites'
jokes.setup: Mac is trying to reconcile the monkey paw with his belief in God
jokes.punchline: His theological framework — God picks winners and smites losers — is delivered with total conviction as profound wisdom
jokes.explanation: Mac's idiosyncratic theology is a reliable vein of comedy for the show. The smiting addendum is a good specific detail that reveals how punitive his version of God is.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: He's very sick. He's, he's dying. He's got leukemia and you shall have a catch with him.

jokes.text: Mac confronts Chase Utley and recites the letter Utley wrote back — including 'I'm sorry your dad doesn't like you. Maybe you could become a better son.'
jokes.setup: Mac ambushes Chase Utley outside his apartment, reciting from memory a letter Utley once sent him
jokes.punchline: The letter, while politely worded, contains 'I'm sorry your dad doesn't like you. Maybe you could become a better son.' — casually devastating
jokes.explanation: Chase Utley (or his assistant) writing 'maybe you could become a better son' in a fan letter is an inspired dark joke. The delivery in formal letter format makes the cruelty funnier. Strong character integration for Mac's father issues, which are a recurring theme. Very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Uncle Jack
dialogue.line: Hey, you want to know my wish, Charlie?

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Sure don't, pal.

jokes.text: Chase Utley thought Mac was a little kid this whole time because of the letters
jokes.setup: Mac reveals he's been writing Chase Utley weekly letters for ten years
jokes.punchline: Utley: 'I thought Mac was a little kid.' — implying the letters read like a child wrote them
jokes.explanation: Good misdirection payoff — Utley's letters have been politely addressing what he thought was a child, making the condescending 'maybe you could become a better son' even darker. Mac's response — inventing a dying son — is a great escalation.

dialogue.speaker: Bonnie
dialogue.line: Well, you could slit Frank's throat with a horn of a goat and drink a bowl of his blood.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: What?

dialogue.speaker: Bonnie
dialogue.line: Well, uh, okay, yeah, maybe not, maybe not that.

jokes.text: Mac invents a dying son named 'Little Mac' on the spot: 'A child born unto me. Little Mac. He's Little Mac, I'm Big Mac, and you shall have a catch with him.'
jokes.setup: Utley thought Mac was a little kid; Mac needs a reason for Utley to have a catch
jokes.punchline: Mac invents a dying child named Little Mac in real time, with the 'Big Mac/Little Mac' naming convention delivered with absolute conviction
jokes.explanation: The 'Big Mac / Little Mac' naming scheme is an inspired absurdist detail that sells the absurdity of the lie. 'A child born unto me' as a biblical phrasing for a fake son is very Mac. The escalation from caught-in-a-lie to fully committed fake-dying-son con is classic Sunny.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: He could behead the gull and wear its skull around his neck for the rest of his life.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Mom, that's not gonna work, 'cause we don't have the gull anymore.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Yeah, we do.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: It is?

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I kicked it under one of the booths so I didn't have to clean it up.

jokes.text: Chase Utley's letter ranks his favorite things: baseball, running fast, and his dad — hair is fourth favorite.
jokes.setup: Mac reads aloud a letter Utley wrote thanking Mac for complimenting his hair.
jokes.punchline: Utley's self-ranking places his own hair fourth among his favorite things — presented without irony as though this is a totally normal thing to rank and share.
jokes.explanation: The specificity of Utley's self-ranking (baseball → running fast → dad → hair) is absurdly funny. 'Running fast' as a discrete category alongside 'my dad' gives the list its comic texture.

dialogue.speaker: Bonnie
dialogue.line: You could give the seagull a proper burial.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: What? Well, yeah, that one, Mom. That one. Why didn't you lead off with that one in the first place?

jokes.text: Chase Utley is unnerved by Mac's hair: 'Your hair, it's throwing me. It's making me very nervous. On the Dodgers, yes, you were the Silver Fox. Philadelphia, you were just the Fox.'
jokes.setup: Chase Utley is processing that Mac is an adult, not a child
jokes.punchline: He delivers a precise taxonomy of his own hair based on his baseball teams — 'Silver Fox' vs. 'Fox' — as if this is the pressing issue
jokes.explanation: Utley's real-player cameo is well-used here — him being weirdly self-aware about his own hair nicknames ('Silver Fox'/'Fox') while ignoring the insane situation with Mac is a good deadpan bit. His comfort with the Fox taxonomy is funny.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Oh, a trophy? From the murder.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Not a... What? No, not a trophy.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Like a souvenir, from your victim.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Not a souvenir, no.

jokes.text: Mac invents leukemia for the fake dying son: 'He's very sick. He's, he's dying. He's got leukemia and you shall have a catch with him.'
jokes.setup: Utley is wavering on the catch; Mac needs to seal the deal
jokes.punchline: Mac pivots to leukemia mid-sentence, delivered in the same earnest tone
jokes.explanation: The pivot to 'leukemia' is dark but fairly expected as an escalation of the dying son con. 'And you shall have a catch with him' as the demand after the leukemia reveal is good — very Mac's formal/absurd phrasing.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Because she's not a cat.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Yeah, but, dude, like, that's-that's the exact kind of thing that could lead to a curse.

jokes.text: Mac threatens to tweet that Utley refused to give a catch to a dying child, then immediately apologizes and admits he threatened him
jokes.setup: Utley hesitates on the catch
jokes.punchline: 'I'll tweet that you didn't.' [Pause] 'I'm sorry. I threatened you. Now I'm upset and so are you. A catch, we shall have? Later today.'
jokes.explanation: Mac's immediate self-awareness after the threat — 'I'm sorry. I threatened you. Now I'm upset and so are you.' — is very funny cringe comedy. The formal phrasing of 'A catch, we shall have? Later today.' as a question-turned-confirmation is delightfully weird. Good character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Cricket
dialogue.line: I can be whatever you want me to be, champ.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Oh, he can.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Would you make it... Do a, do a turn. Do a spin.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: There you go. Make it sexy. Let's go.

jokes.text: Uncle Jack's birthday party is happening at Charlie's mom's house when Charlie and Frank arrive for supernatural consultation
jokes.setup: Charlie and Frank go to Charlie's mom for expertise on sailor curses
jokes.punchline: Charlie forgot it's Uncle Jack's birthday — the consultation has to happen at a birthday party with Uncle Jack present
jokes.explanation: Functional setup for the Uncle Jack cringe bits to follow. The birthday party context is more of a vehicle than a joke in itself.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Well, ever since I found this monkey's paw, my luck has totally turned around. Well, actually, it wasn't just a paw. It was a whole monkey behind the kegs, and he was dead.

jokes.text: Uncle Jack tries to hold hands with Charlie during the birthday candle wish — 'you and I hold hands' — Charlie's immediate 'Nope'
jokes.setup: Everyone is about to watch Uncle Jack blow out birthday candles
jokes.punchline: Uncle Jack turns to Charlie and says 'you and I hold hands' — Charlie's flat 'Nope' is the punchline
jokes.explanation: Classic Uncle Jack discomfort beat. The economy of 'Nope' as Charlie's total response is excellent. The handholding request at a birthday candle ceremony is very specific and very wrong in a funny way.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: That's probably the monkey that worked here, robbed us and fucked our faces.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: He got stuck behind the keg.

jokes.text: Frank tries to make a birthday wish by blowing on the candles even though it's not his birthday
jokes.setup: Uncle Jack is blowing out his birthday candles
jokes.punchline: Frank announces 'I made a wish, too' — having also blown on the candles — and suggests going upstairs with 'Bon' (Charlie's Mom)
jokes.explanation: Frank's total disregard for birthday ritual etiquette is in character, and the implied wish (going upstairs with Charlie's mom) is suitably gross. Not the sharpest version of the Frank/Charlie's Mom running gag.

dialogue.speaker: Chase
dialogue.line: But actions do have consequences. Like lying, Mac. Why don't you hand over that monkey paw?

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Hall of Fame, baby, here I come!

jokes.text: Charlie's mom's first two curse remedies: (1) slit Frank's throat with a goat horn and drink his blood, (2) behead the gull and wear its skull around his neck forever
jokes.setup: Charlie asks if there's anything that can be done about the curse
jokes.punchline: She offers two remedies — throat slitting/blood drinking and permanent gull skull necklace — before arriving at 'a proper burial'
jokes.explanation: The escalating curse remedies — from extreme (blood drinking) to merely grotesque (skull necklace) — before arriving at 'proper burial' as the obviously correct answer is well-structured. The fact that Charlie has to ask 'why didn't you lead with that one?' is a perfect button on the sequence.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Well, is it possible, Frank, that that egg was a seagull egg?

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Oh...

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: That might've been, because, you know what, we found some eggs...

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I might've swapped...

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: You did a flip-flop.

jokes.text: Second remedy: 'He could behead the gull and wear its skull around his neck for the rest of his life.' / Frank: 'I don't know. Could be cool.'
jokes.setup: Charlie's Mom offers a second alternative to murdering Frank.
jokes.punchline: Frank genuinely considers wearing a seagull skull necklace for life as a viable option — 'Could be cool.'
jokes.explanation: Frank's 'Could be cool' is perfect — delivered with genuine, open-minded consideration of permanent seagull-skull jewelry. His aesthetic neutrality toward the grotesque is a great character beat.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: We're just the type of people to bury various animals and-and wives in a pet cemetery when we know we should be at work.

jokes.text: Frank says he wants to wear the gull skull: 'I don't know. Could be cool.'
jokes.setup: Charlie rejects the gull skull necklace remedy as crazy
jokes.punchline: Frank considers it seriously: 'I don't know. Could be cool.'
jokes.explanation: Four words that say everything about Frank's character — his complete lack of normal social calibration, his openness to genuinely weird aesthetic choices. Excellent economy.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I don't know, Cricks, I guess... there's no real explanation as to why bad things would happen to you.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Maybe it's just one of those things, Cricket.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: That's life.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: You got a dark cloud following you around.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: It is what it is.

jokes.text: Charlie asks his mom 'Do I look like I'm at sea, Mom?' / Mom: 'I don't know.'
jokes.setup: Charlie's mom explains the burial option might not always be available 'if you're at sea'
jokes.punchline: Charlie asks 'Do I look like I'm at sea?' — his mom genuinely doesn't know the answer
jokes.explanation: Charlie's mom's genuine uncertainty about whether her son might be at sea is a great character beat — it implies she has very little grip on Charlie's daily life. The mutual bafflement is funny.

jokes.text: Uncle Jack puts his hand on Charlie; Charlie repeatedly tells him to stop
jokes.setup: The birthday consultation is winding down
jokes.punchline: Uncle Jack silently keeps touching Charlie; Charlie's escalating 'Stop. Stop putting your hand on me.' while trying to have a serious conversation
jokes.explanation: A reliable Uncle Jack cringe beat. Less precise than the 'Sure don't, pal' joke but functions well as a running gag payoff.

jokes.text: Frank reveals he has been keeping Maureen Ponderosa's ashes at the bar — first calling it a 'trophy,' then 'souvenir from the murder,' then correcting to 'way to spite her'
jokes.setup: While looking for the dead seagull under the booth, they find a container that turns out to be Maureen Ponderosa's ashes
jokes.punchline: Frank's successive attempts to describe why he has his dead wife's ashes ('trophy,' 'souvenir from your victim,' 'way to spite her') each being worse than the last
jokes.explanation: The escalating descriptors for why Frank has his dead wife's ashes — trophy, murder souvenir, spite vessel — each carrying a different degree of psychopathy, is excellent dark comedy. Charlie's straight-man 'like a souvenir from your victim' is perfectly deadpan. Very dark, very Frank, well-structured.

jokes.text: Frank refused his wife Maureen's dying wish to be buried in a pet cemetery 'because she's not a cat'
jokes.setup: It emerges that Frank has Maureen's ashes and hasn't buried her
jokes.punchline: He denied her dying wish of a pet cemetery burial because 'she's not a cat' — completely missing the point of personal wishes
jokes.explanation: 'She's not a cat' as the totality of Frank's reasoning for denying his dying wife's burial wishes is pitch-perfect Frank logic — technically true, completely beside the point, and callous beyond measure. Excellent economy and character integration.

jokes.text: Cricket's 'kid' for Mac's dying son scheme turns out to be a grown adult junkie sex worker who does a spin on command
jokes.setup: Cricket was supposed to find a 'kid' to play Mac's dying son for Chase Utley
jokes.punchline: He brings a visibly adult, visibly intoxicated man who does a 'sexy spin' on Cricket's instruction; Cricket defends: 'his name on the street is literally Kid'
jokes.explanation: Classic Sunny escalation — Cricket's good intentions producing the worst possible outcome. The 'sexy spin' detail makes it specific and funny. 'His name on the street is literally Kid' is a perfect deflection that reveals Cricket's completely different operational reality.

jokes.text: Mac describes Cricket's operation: 'I believe that Cricket is now a pimp, and that was his boy slut.'
jokes.setup: The gang watches in confusion as Cricket's 'kid' does a sexy spin and is ushered out
jokes.punchline: Mac's clinical, matter-of-fact assessment: 'Cricket is now a pimp, and that was his boy slut'
jokes.explanation: Mac's detached, matter-of-fact delivery of a genuinely dark assessment is very funny. 'That's oversimplifying it. But that's it in a nutshell' from Cricket is an excellent button that confirms while slightly hedging. Good economy.

jokes.text: Mac's summary: 'I believe that Cricket is now a pimp, and that was his boy slut.' Cricket: 'Uh, t-that's oversimplifying it. But, uh, that's-that's it in a nutshell.'
jokes.setup: The gang is trying to understand what Cricket's business model is.
jokes.punchline: Cricket objects to 'oversimplifying' — but then confirms it's accurate. The objection to the label while accepting the substance is the joke.
jokes.explanation: 'That's oversimplifying it. But that's it in a nutshell.' is a great Cricket line — his dignity demands nuance, but he can't actually provide any. The gap between his self-perception and reality is the engine of his character.

jokes.text: Charlie reveals the monkey paw came from a dead monkey that had been behind the bar's kegs, with cash in its hand — 'the monkey that worked here, robbed us and fucked our faces'
jokes.setup: Mac explains the lucky monkey paw that's been bringing him good luck
jokes.punchline: Charlie identifies it as the monkey from a previous episode/event who worked at the bar and robbed them — it decomposed behind the kegs after getting stuck there
jokes.explanation: The reveal that the lucky monkey paw belongs to a known monkey who had a whole arc with the gang — robbing them, 'fucking their faces,' dying behind the kegs — is excellent series mythology comedy. 'The monkey that worked here, robbed us and fucked our faces' is an extraordinary sentence delivered completely casually. High rewatch bonus for fans of the series.

jokes.text: 'Well, he is decomposing and there's also a shit-ton of mold back there. / Shit, now I smell it. / I don't know how I missed that.'
jokes.setup: The gang has just learned about the dead monkey behind the kegs
jokes.punchline: The confirmation that there's decomposition AND massive mold — and that everyone can suddenly smell it — lands as a cascade of reactions
jokes.explanation: 'I don't know how I missed that' is funny as genuine puzzlement — these people have been breathing this air. Also seeds the mold-explains-everything reveal. Good reaction cascade.

jokes.text: Mac and Charlie both independently kicked rotting things under/behind furniture rather than cleaning them: Mac kicked the gull under a booth, Mac kicked the monkey behind the kegs
jokes.setup: It turns out both the dead seagull and the dead monkey were kicked to hidden locations rather than dealt with
jokes.punchline: 'I kicked it under one of the booths so I didn't feel like cleaning it up.' / 'I found him by the office, but I kicked him behind the kegs because I didn't feel like cleaning him up.' — the gang's universal approach to corpse management
jokes.explanation: The escalating revelation that multiple gang members have been kicking dead things to hidden locations rather than cleaning them is a great running gag that reveals the bar's true state. The parallel construction (both use 'I kicked it somewhere because I didn't feel like cleaning it up') is structurally tidy.

jokes.text: The gang discovers the dead monkey, dead seagull, and dead wife's ashes have all been accumulating at the bar because nobody wanted to clean them up.
jokes.setup: Mac reveals the monkey is behind the kegs.
jokes.punchline: Both Mac and Charlie independently say they kicked their respective bodies (monkey, seagull) behind/under things rather than deal with them — and Frank has been storing his dead wife's ashes in the bar.
jokes.explanation: The structural payoff of multiple independent threads converging — everyone's been kicking bodies behind furniture instead of dealing with them — is very well executed. The simultaneous revelation that the bar contains a dead monkey, dead seagull, and human ashes, all from negligence, is a great escalating convergence gag.

jokes.text: Charlie's new plan: bury Maureen's ashes, the seagull, and 'what's left of the monkey' together in a pet cemetery — a mass burial of humans and animals
jokes.setup: Charlie tries to find a solution that satisfies all the curses simultaneously
jokes.punchline: He proposes a combined burial: a dead wife, a seagull, and a decomposed monkey — all in a pet cemetery, honoring Maureen's wish, lifting the sailor curse, and disposing of the monkey
jokes.explanation: Charlie's characteristically pragmatic/insane solution — why not just bury everything together? — is a great convergence of all the episode's plot threads. The logic is both completely wrong and weirdly reasonable, which is peak Charlie.

jokes.text: Mac tells Chase Utley that the dying son is dead: 'He was only ten years old when he died. He's dead now.'
jokes.setup: Mac arrives at the pet cemetery with Chase Utley for the catch with his 'dying son'
jokes.punchline: 'He was only ten years old when he died. He's dead now.' — the redundant 'He's dead now' as if clarifying
jokes.explanation: 'He's dead now' as a clarifying addendum to 'he died' is a good comedic redundancy. The sheer audacity of the escalation — Mac bringing Chase Utley to an actual cemetery for a fake son — is well-executed.

jokes.text: Chase Utley: 'Why is he buried at a pet cemetery?' / Mac: 'Dogs. He loved dogs.'
jokes.setup: Utley notices the obviously odd choice of burial location for a human child
jokes.punchline: 'Dogs. He loved dogs.' — delivered with complete conviction as if that's a satisfying explanation
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the episode. 'Dogs. He loved dogs.' is perfect economy — two sentences, maximum absurdity. It's the kind of answer that is simultaneously the least satisfying and most confident answer to the question. Mac's total commitment to the lie with a completely inadequate explanation is brilliant character comedy. Very quotable.

jokes.text: Mac confesses the monkey paw and superstition logic to Chase Utley, who responds with a sincere baseball philosophy about belief affecting action
jokes.setup: Mac admits everything to Utley, expecting to be dismissed
jokes.punchline: Utley validates superstitions completely sincerely — 'How do you think baseball players get out of their slumps? With superstitions.' — but then uses it to pivot to a lecture on Mac's dishonesty
jokes.explanation: Utley's sincerity about superstitions is an unexpected reversal that works. The pivot from validating Mac to calling out his lying is structurally clean. Less a traditional joke than a character scene with comedic payoff.

jokes.text: Chase Utley steals the monkey paw and runs off to the Hall of Fame
jokes.setup: Utley has just delivered a sincere lecture about honesty and consequences — Mac hands over the monkey paw
jokes.punchline: Utley pockets the paw and sprints off yelling 'Hall of Fame, baby, here I come!' — completely abandoning his moral high ground the instant he has the paw
jokes.explanation: The best punchline in the episode. The setup is perfect — Utley has just delivered a sincere speech about honesty and consequences, Mac is emotionally affected, and then Utley instantly steals the paw and bolts. 'Hall of Fame, baby, here I come!' is an inspired specific detail (Utley's real-world Hall of Fame eligibility/candidacy makes this bite harder). The complete betrayal of his just-established moral character in one instant is a masterpiece of misdirection. High rewatch bonus, highly quotable.

jokes.text: The rational explanation: Dee's facial paralysis was mold exposure, not a curse — 'temporary facial paralysis and brain fog are symptoms of exposure to high levels of mold'
jokes.setup: The gang has been operating under curse logic all episode
jokes.punchline: The reveal that all the supernatural events have a mundane explanation: mold poisoning from the dead monkey decomposing behind the kegs
jokes.explanation: The structural payoff of the episode — everything that seemed supernatural (word-finding problems, Bell's palsy, silverfish, the bloody egg) has been building toward a mundane mold-poisoning explanation. Giving all the brain fog moments rewatch value. Well-structured episode-long misdirection with a satisfying logical reveal.

jokes.text: The bloody egg was a seagull egg Frank mixed up with his store eggs
jokes.setup: The gang is working backward through all the 'cursed' events
jokes.punchline: 'Is it possible, Frank, that egg was a seagull egg?' / 'That might've been, because we found some eggs and we had store eggs and you might've mixed them up.' / 'You did a flip-flop.'
jokes.explanation: A satisfying callback payoff — the mysterious bloody egg was just a seagull egg Frank mixed with his store eggs. 'You did a flip-flop' as the gang's euphemism for mixing up seagull eggs and regular eggs is oddly specific and funny.

jokes.text: Mac concludes they're 'still cursed' because they missed Bar Rescue despite the mundane explanations for everything
jokes.setup: The gang has rationally explained away every 'curse' — no supernatural forces at work
jokes.punchline: Mac reads the rejection letter from Bar Rescue and concludes: 'So that means we are still cursed.'
jokes.explanation: A good structural button — the gang's self-delusion causes them to miss Bar Rescue, then Mac reinstates the curse narrative to explain away their self-caused failure. Classic Sunny: the gang is always the architect of their own disasters.

jokes.text: Dennis's correction to Mac: 'Mac, no, you were never lucky. You just bombarded them both with mail. And you stalked Chase Utley for years.'
jokes.setup: Mac blames the lost monkey paw for missing Bar Rescue
jokes.punchline: Dennis's lucid assessment: everything good that happened was the result of obsessive, years-long mail campaigns and stalking, not luck
jokes.explanation: A good closing observation that reframes 'luck' as 'unhinged persistence.' Dennis's occasional moments of genuine clarity about the gang's behavior are always welcome. The juxtaposition of 'not lucky, just stalking' is a satisfying ironic reversal.

jokes.text: Dennis's final speech: 'We're just the type of people to bury various animals and wives in a pet cemetery when we know we should be at work.'
jokes.setup: The gang is wrapping up the episode's failures
jokes.punchline: 'We're just the type of people to bury various animals and wives in a pet cemetery when we know we should be at work.'
jokes.explanation: A great closing line that encapsulates the entire episode in one sentence. 'Various animals and wives' is perfect — the casual lumping of Maureen in with the animals is very dark. The 'when we know we should be at work' is the perfect bathetic anchor. Highly quotable, economical, and earns its place as the episode's thesis statement.

jokes.text: The gang's response to Cricket asking about his luck: 'there's no real explanation as to why bad things would happen to you... It is what it is.' — delivered with cheerful indifference
jokes.setup: Cricket asks what about his bad luck — hoping to be included in the group's resolution
jokes.punchline: The entire gang casually dismisses Cricket's misfortune as unexplainable and inevitable: 'It is what it is' repeated multiple times over each other, with someone noting 'Nice day.'
jokes.explanation: A perfect dark comedy button for Cricket's character — the gang's complete inability to engage with Cricket's genuine suffering, overlapping 'it is what it is' dismissals, and the final 'Nice day' non-sequitur perfectly captures how they treat Cricket. The cheerful indifference to his perpetual misfortune is the entire Cricket arc in miniature. 'You got a dark cloud following you around' as a diagnosis delivered casually is excellent.

tmdb_overview: The Gang’s going to be on Bar Rescue but a series of bad omens leads them to believe they are all cursed. They set off to undo the curses and make amends to those they’ve wronged, while Mac, who’s on a run of good luck, meets Chase Utley and invites him for a catch.
